ShorterBetter: Guiding Reasoning Models to Find Optimal Inference Length for Efficient Reasoning

Jingyang Yi Affiliation: University of Chicago Email: jingyang22@uchicago.edu    Jiazheng Wang Affiliation: University of Chicago Email: jiazhengw@uchicago.edu
Abstract

Reasoning models such as OpenAI o3 and DeepSeek-R1 have demonstrated strong performance on reasoning-intensive tasks through extended Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting. While longer reasoning traces can facilitate a more thorough exploration of solution paths for complex problems, researchers have observed that these models often “overthink”, leading to inefficient inference. In this paper, we introduce ShorterBetter, a simple yet effective reinforcement learning methed that enables reasoning language models to discover their own optimal CoT lengths without human intervention. By sampling multiple outputs per problem and defining the Sample Optimal Length (SOL) as the shortest correct response among all the outputs, our method dynamically guides the model toward optimal inference lengths. Applied to the DeepSeek-Distill-Qwen-1.5B model, ShorterBetter achieves up to an 80% reduction in output length on both in-domain and out-of-domain reasoning tasks while maintaining accuracy. Our analysis shows that overly long reasoning traces often reflect loss of reasoning direction, and thus suggests that the extended CoT produced by reasoning models is highly compressible.

1 Introduction

Leveraging the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) has recently improved the performance of models such as OpenAI-o1 (OpenAI, 2024) and DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek-AI, 2025) across various benchmarks. Specifically, through reinforcement learning, these models have developed the ability to produce intermediate reasoning Chain-of-Thought (Wei et al., 2022) steps before giving the final answer, including explicit reasoning steps and reflective processes such as self-verification and experimentation with alternative problem-solving strategies. This enhances LLMs’ ability to handle complex logic and demonstrate human-like problem-solving behaviors.

Although DeepSeek-R1 and its distilled model family (DeepSeek-AI, 2025) demonstrates improved performance as the reasoning length increases, we argue that many current reasoning models exhibit overthinking behavior and do not always require such lengthy reasoning to achieve correct answers. Moreover, the enhanced reasoning steps come at a steep computational cost. To better understand this limitation, we present examples of observed model behaviors that motivate the need for a mechanism to find an optimal reasoning length and shorten the reasoning process, thereby reducing unnecessary steps and improving efficiency:

  • •

    Repetitive Self-Verification in Intermediate Steps: Models frequently verify intermediate results repeatedly, even when these verifications do not provide additional value, thus increasing redundancy and computation time.

  • •

    Continued Exploration of Alternative Strategies After Correct Solution: Models may unnecessarily continue exploring alternative problem-solving methods even after obtaining the correct solution, wasting computational resources.

  • •

    Early Stop of Reasoning Paths: Models occasionally interrupt effective reasoning processes to explore alternative strategies, potentially abandoning a correct approach and reducing overall efficiency.

  • •

    Model Collapse After Excessively Long Output: The model’s output will break down and produce meaningless and unstructured text.

To address this problem, recent works have attempted to find the optimal length of the reasoning process for a given problem (Yang et al., 2025), which ideally should be a number that varies and adapts to the problem’s intrinsic difficulty. O1-Pruner (Luo et al., 2025a) and L1 (Aggarwal and Welleck, 2025) both modified the original GRPO framework (Shao et al., 2024) to constrain the model’s output length based on a user-defined token length in the prompt. While these methods grant direct control over CoT length, they depend on manually selected budgets and relies on human’s estimation on each problem’s difficulty. In this work, we hypothesize that reinforcement learning can enable the model to discover its own optimal length. Specifically, for each problem, we generate multiple outputs and define the sample optimal length (SOL) as the length of the shortest correct response. We then use SOL to iteratively guide the model toward its optimal output length. This approach removes the need for manual length constraints or predefined stopping criteria, allowing the model to internalize an efficient reasoning strategy based on task performance. By learning to balance brevity and correctness, the model reduces unnecessary steps, improving both inference efficiency and output quality.

2 Related Work

Reasoning in Large Language Models

Recent advancements in inference-time scaling strategies for LLMs—particularly those that incorporate intermediate reasoning outputs—have substantially improved performance on complex tasks. Early efforts in this direction include Chain-of-Thought style prompting (Wei et al., 2022; Yao et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024; Meng et al., 2024) to decompose the problem to subtask-solving, and fine-tuning with budget forcing (Muennighoff et al., 2025). More recently, reinforcement learning-based approaches, such as RLHF (Ouyang et al., 2022) and GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), have gained prominence for enhancing reasoning capabilities. Notable examples of reasoning-augmented LLMs include OpenAI o1 (OpenAI, 2024), DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek-AI, 2025), and QwQ (Yang et al., 2024), where reasoning skills naturally emerge during the reinforcement learning phase. Although output length is not explicitly rewarded, these models implicitly learn that producing longer, more thorough reasoning traces leads to higher task accuracy, and thus greater reward (Shao et al., 2024). Consequently, they autonomously develop the ability to generate extended, detailed reasoning processes.

Efficient LLM Reasoning

While Chain-of-Thought prompting (Wei et al., 2022) and Inference Scaling (Muennighoff et al., 2025) substantially improve the ability of large language models (LLMs) to tackle complex tasks, they often introduce significant computational overhead and an overthinking phenomenon (Chen et al., 2024). Recent work further shows that longer reasoning chains are not always beneficial: Fatemi et al. (2025) find that excessive reasoning can degrade logical correctness and introduce irrelevant information, while Wu et al. (2025) argue that performance peaks at an optimal number of reasoning steps, after which additional steps accumulate errors and noise. As a result, research is increasingly focused on making LLM reasoning more concise and efficient. Luo et al. (2025a) and Aggarwal and Welleck (2025) modify the GRPO reward function (Shao et al., 2024) to control output length according to a predefined token budget. Fatemi et al. (2025) use a two-phase Proximal Policy Optimization (Schulman et al., 2017) approach, adjusting reasoning length based on problem difficulty. Xia et al. (2025) prune reasoning traces by identifying and preserving only the tokens critical to the final answer. In contrast to these methods, our approach enables the model to adaptively discover the optimal reasoning length for each question, without relying on externally specified constraints.

LLM Self-Play

Recent work explores enabling LLMs to improve through self-play, without relying solely on external feedback. In this setting, the model uses its own capabilities to generate training data and even reward signals. Gulcehre et al. (2023) sample outputs from the current model, filter them to build a dataset, and fine-tune using offline RL methods. Kiruluta et al. (2025) propose CAGSR, where the model generates multiple candidate responses per prompt, records cross-attention patterns, and scores candidates using a self-supervised reward based on these patterns, updating the model with PPO. Kumar et al. () design a reward structure that incentivizes self-correction—penalizing correct-to-incorrect changes while providing no reward for maintaining correctness or incorrectness. Wu et al. (2024) further reduce reliance on human feedback by letting the model learn from its own assessments. Our method draws inspiration from these self-play strategies by generating multiple outputs and rewarding the shortest correct response.

3 Method

Our goal is to guide the reasoning model to determine the optimal inference length for a given problem. A primary challenge is the absence of prior knowledge regarding the optimal inference length that suits the current prompt. Ideally, this length would depend on the model’s capabilities and the inherent difficulty of the problem itself, making it challenging to designate a predetermined inference length for each individual case. To overcome this issue, we introduce a simple yet effective reinforcement learning approach that incentivizes the model to autonomously discover optimal inference lengths through on-policy learning.

Finding the Sample Optimal Length (SOL)

We define the sample optimal length (SOL) for each group of model outputs as follows: if at least one response in the group is correct, SOL is set to the length of the shortest correct response; otherwise, SOL is the mean length of all sampled responses. Given this definition, our method generates multiple candidate responses per query and assigns each a reward that combines its correctness with its deviation from the SOL. We employ Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024) to optimize under these group-relative rewards, encouraging the model to discover and settle on the most concise correct reasoning length without relying on externally imposed “gold-standard” lengths.

Formally, given a problem, the policy model generates nn responses to form a sample group, denoting G={o1,o2,…,on}G=\{o_{1},o_{2},\dots,o_{n}\}. Let ℓ⁡(oi)\ell(o_{i}) denote the length of response oio_{i} (measured in tokens). The reward for each generated response oio_{i} is defined as:

ri=α​𝕀​(y^i=yg​t)−β​|ℓ∗​(G)−ℓ⁡(oi)|,r_{i}=\alpha\mathbb{I}(\hat{y}_{i}=y_{gt})-\beta|\ell^{*}(G)-\ell(o_{i})|,

where α\alpha and β\beta are hyper-parameters, and 𝕀⁡(⋅)\mathbb{I}(\cdot) denotes the indicator function. yi^\hat{y_{i}} denotes the extracted final answer from oio_{i}. yg​ty_{gt} denotes the ground truth answer. The sample optimal length, ℓ∗​(G)\ell^{*}(G), is defined as:

ℓ∗​(G)={min⁡{ℓ⁡(oi)∣𝕀⁡(yi=yg​t)=1},if at least one correct response exists in ​G,1n​∑i=1nℓ⁡(oi),otherwise.\ell^{*}(G)=\begin{cases}\min\left\{\ell(o_{i})\mid\mathbb{I}(y_{i}=y_{gt})=1\right\},&\text{if at least one correct response exists in }G,\\[6.0pt] \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell(o_{i}),&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

Here, the hyper-parameters α\alpha and β\beta control the relative magnitude of the correctness reward and the length penalty, respectively. In our experiments, we observed that a larger α\alpha helps stabilize accuracy rates after the initial training phase, during which inference lengths typically decrease rapidly. Conversely, a larger β\beta accelerates length reduction but risks triggering length hacking, which can negatively affect response accuracy. Additionally, increasing the group size nn broadens the search space for optimal inference lengths.

It’s worth noting that in the reward function, length penalty term does not incorporate any normalization or length reference, unlike other reinforcement learning-based methods (Arora and Zanette, 2025; Luo et al., 2025a). Besides, we choose to decouple the correctness reward and the length penalty so that the model will always be penalized for deviating from SOL, regardless of whether the output is correct or not. In contrast, a multiplicative formulation would diminish the impact of length penalties for incorrect responses. In our experiments, we observe that this simple design helps the model consistently shorten its output lengths while ensuring that such improvements remain tied to correct reasoning.

During training, the choice of SOL inherently combines the embeddings of the correct and shortest response. In Section 5.3, we present an ablation study showing that our method still performs well even when the correctness term is entirely removed from the reward function, i.e., setting α=0\alpha=0.

Search for optimal length without human intervention.

Our reward function is designed to guide the model toward producing the shortest possible inference traces without compromising accuracy. The key innovation of our approach lies in the dynamic nature of the sample optimal length, ℓ∗​(G)\ell^{*}(G), which adapts automatically to both the difficulty of the input problem and the model’s current reasoning ability—without requiring any human intervention. To enable the model to learn such adaptive inference lengths, it is essential to train on a diverse set of problems spanning a wide range of difficulty levels. This variety ensures that the model develops the flexibility to tailor its reasoning depth appropriately across different tasks.

4 Experimental Setup

Datasets and Models

To encourage flexible inference lengths, we train our model on problems spanning a wide range of difficulty levels. We perform reinforcement learning fine-tuning on DeepScaleR (Luo et al., 2025b), a benchmark of 40 K mathematical problems drawn from AIME, AMC, Omni-MATH (Gao et al., 2024), and the Still dataset (Min et al., 2024). This mixed dataset covers tasks from high-school math problems to Olympiad-level challenges. As our base reasoning model, we use DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (DeepSeek-AI, 2025), which has demonstrated strong performance on complex problems via extended Chain-of-Thought reasoning. We further validate our approach on the 7B variant of this distilled model. Larger models benefit from higher baseline accuracy, yielding more correct samples per generated sample and thus more reliable estimation of the sample optimal length.

Evaluations

We evaluate the trained model on held-out subsets of the training math datasets. Additionally, we assess the out-of-domain generalization of our method on a set of reasoning-intensive benchmarks, including MathQA (Amini et al., 2019) MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021), Big-Bench Hard (Suzgun et al., 2022) and LiveCodeBench (Jain et al., 2024). We use accuracy and output length (in tokens) as our evaluation metrics. All tasks are evaluated in a zero-shot setting without any prompting techniques. Since our test tasks all have clear ground truths, we use rule-based methods to evaluate the results. We allocate a budget of 8000 tokens when evaluating DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and 16000 tokens for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B.

Implementation Details

We used Verl (Sheng et al., 2024), an open-source reinforcement learning (RL) training library, as our GRPO framework. We fine-tuned our 1.5B base models with a batch size of 64 and a rollout group size of 8. Training was conducted for 300 steps with a fixed learning rate of 1×10−61\times 10^{-6}. For the 7B variant, because the larger model converges more quickly due to its higher baseline accuracy, we trained for only 200 steps. To save computational resources, we set a maximum inference length of 6,000 tokens for the 1.5B model and 5,000 tokens for the 7B model. These constraints only affect the early stages of training, as the mean inference lengths quickly drop below the limits. Finally, to study the effect of hyper-parameters, we compared two 1.5B variants with α=1\alpha=1 and α=2\alpha=2, while keeping β=0.001\beta=0.001 fixed. Setting β=0.001\beta=0.001 means that every 1,000-token deviation from the SOL results in a reward penalty of −1-1.

We set n=8n=8 for all experiments in the main results, meaning the model generates 8 completions for each prompt during training. However, prior experiments show that setting n=4n=4 also achieves similar performance, although with a slightly slower convergence rate. This suggests that our method is not sensitive to the choice of nn, further highlighting its computational efficiency.

Baselines

To evaluate the efficiency of our method, we compare against two baselines: (1) DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/7B and (2) Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B-Instruct (Team, 2024). The DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen models are distilled from the larger DeepSeek-R1 architecture (DeepSeek-AI, 2025). The first baseline assesses inference length—our goal is to significantly shorten outputs while preserving task accuracy. The second baseline measures reasoning capability—ideally, our trained models achieve inference lengths on par with the instruct models but with much higher accuracy. Together, these comparisons demonstrate that our approach delivers superior inference efficiency relative to both distilled and instruct baselines.

5 Results and Discussion

In this section, we present and analyze the effectiveness of our proposed method. We compare the performance of our trained models against the baselines across a range of math tasks as well as out-of-domain benchmarks. We then provide an in-depth analysis of how our method guides the model to discover optimal inference lengths and discuss why excessively long Chain-of-Thought (CoT) traces may indicate a loss of direction in reasoning.

5.1 Experimental Results

Our method significantly reduces inference length while maintaining strong performance

We compare the performance of the 1.5B model trained with our method against baseline models, as shown in Figure 2. We report results for two variants, using α=1\alpha=1 and α=2\alpha=2, where a higher α\alpha places greater weight on correctness in the reward. Both variants outperform the distilled reasoning model and the instruct model of the same size. Specifically, the α=1\alpha=1 model and α=2\alpha=2 model achieve average inference length reductions of 77.6% and 79.2%, with corresponding changes in accuracy of +2.5 % and +3.2 %, respectively. More comprehensive experiment results including 7B model performances are shown in Table 1. These results demonstrate that our method effectively reduces overthinking in reasoning models while preserving accuracy rates. Compared to the instruct model, our method yields much higher accuracy and comparable output lengths. Our approach strikes a meaningful balance between underthinking and overthinking, particularly in challenging reasoning tasks. This balance is made possible by our reinforcement learning framework, which uses SOL to iteratively guide the model toward efficient inference.

Our method generalizes well to out-of-domain tasks

We further evaluate our method on a diverse set of reasoning tasks that were not part of the training data, including general reasoning, math, question answering, and coding benchmarks. Despite being trained exclusively on math problems, our model generalizes remarkably well to these out-of-domain settings. Compared to the distilled reasoning model, the α=1\alpha=1 and α=2\alpha=2 variants achieve average length reductions of 77.0 % and 75.5 % , with corresponding changes in accuracy of –0.8 % and –1.6 %, respectively.

Notably, across different tasks, our models achieve varying levels of length reduction. In general reasoning tasks such as BBH and MMLU, the trained model produces average outputs of fewer than 300 tokens, resulting in more than an 80% reduction in output length compared to the distill model (even shorter than the instruct model). In contrast, on harder benchmarks like LiveCodeBench, the models generate outputs with an average length of about 5,000 tokens, achieving a 50% reduction. These results demonstrate that our method enables the model to adjust its output length dynamically based on the nature of the problem, rather than aiming for a fixed reduction target.

The strong performance across both in-domain and out-of-domain tasks demonstrates two key insights: (1) our method achieves length reduction by eliminating unnecessary reasoning steps, (e.g. repetitive self-verification) or verbose phrasing, without compromising the essential reasoning process (we will further discuss this in the following section); and (2) extended Chain-of-Thought traces are highly compressible.

5.2 Analysis of the Results

Effectively guide the model to find optimal inference lengths

On the left side of Figure 3, we illustrate how the model learns to identify optimal inference lengths throughout training. For each sample generation (n=8n=8) of a given problem, we compute the SOL and take the batch-wise average. We also track the mean deviation of individual outputs from their respective SOL, defined as di=ℓi−ℓ∗​(G)ℓ∗​(G)d_{i}=\frac{\ell_{i}-\ell^{*}(G)}{\ell^{*}(G)}. For instance, a deviation of 0.2 at a given training step indicates that the generated outputs deviate from the optimal length by 20% on average. The plots show that both the SOL and the mean deviation steadily decrease over training, particularly within the first 100 steps. This trend suggests that reinforcement learning is successfully guiding the model to produce outputs that cluster towards to the optimal length.

Longer CoT lengths imply loss of direction during reasoning

Contrary to the common assumption that longer Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning (i.e., test-time scaling) leads to better performance, we argue that in models trained with rule-based reinforcement learning, longer reasoning does not always correspond to better results.

(1) Extended CoTs are highly compressible: our trained models achieved substantial reductions in output length while maintaining strong accuracy, and qualitative analysis confirms that the post-trained models produce significantly less verbose outputs.

(2) Long CoTs can signal a loss of direction during reasoning due to several reasons. As shown on the right-hand side of Figure 2, we conducted an experiment using 150 problems (30 each from AIME, AMC, MATH, Olympiad-bench, and Minerva). For each problem, we generated 10 responses with the DeepSeek-distilled Qwen models. We filtered out problems that all responses were correct or all responses were wrong to exclude trivial or unsolvable cases. We then computed the difference between the average lengths of correct and incorrect responses to form a length gap distribution. The results show that, on average, for the same problem, incorrect responses are significantly longer than correct ones—by 5,541 tokens on the 1.5B model and 5,910 tokens on the 7B model. Similar results were observed in the instruct models. This suggests a clear correlation between reasoning errors and unnecessarily long CoT traces.

5.3 Ablation Tests

Sample optimal length inherently combines correctness and conciseness

To validate the key design of our method, sample optimal length, we conducted two experiments to demonstrate that SOL is essential to the effectiveness of our approach, as shown in Figure 4. The first experiment removes the entire design of SOL: (1) there is no reward for correctness, and (2) the target length for each sample group is selected as the shortest response, regardless of correctness, that is, ℓ∗​(G)=min⁡ℓ⁡(oi)\ell^{*}(G)=\min{\ell(o_{i})}. In the second experiment, we set the correctness reward to zero (α=0\alpha=0) but still adopt SOL as our sample target length.

The ablation test results clearly show that if we simply select the shortest response length as the sample target length, regardless of correctness, the training process quickly collapses, with both output length and accuracy converging to zero. However, if we discard only the correctness term in the reward function, the training still runs successfully, although with more fluctuations in accuracy. Notably, after 150 steps, the output lengths even increased. These results suggest that SOL inherently combines correctness and conciseness.

6 Conclusion

In this work, we introduced ShorterBetter, an efficient and effective reinforcement learning-based approach that substantially reduces redundant Chain-of-Thought reasoning in language models while preserving response accuracy. In contrast to existing length-rewarding RL methods, our key innovation is the use of the sample optimal length, i.e. the shortest correct response within a sampled group, as a dynamic, self-supervised signal to guide the model toward optimal inference length. This design removes the need for any predefined length targets or curated training datasets.

Our method is simple to implement and computationally efficient. Experiments demonstrate that our post-trained models retain strong reasoning performance on math tasks while achieving up to an 80% reduction in inference length. Moreover, the trained models generalize effectively to out-of-domain tasks, including commonsense reasoning, logical inference, and code generation. These results challenge the assumption that longer reasoning traces (i.e. test-time scaling) are inherently beneficial. Instead, we show that if a model already has sufficient reasoning capability, its extended Chain-of-Thought outputs are often highly compressible.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
